sections.heading: What does an underactive thyroid feel like?
sections.body:
An underactive thyroid develops slowly, and symptoms may not show for months or even years. Because the changes build up gradually, some people do not realise there is a problem for several years. The NHS lists common symptoms such as feeling very tired, putting on weight, feeling colder than usual and constipation. Poor concentration, low mood, dry skin, hair loss and a hoarse voice are also described, and some people have irregular or heavy periods.

Symptoms can differ from one person to the next. Many of these problems have other explanations, so a blood test that measures hormone levels is the only accurate way to confirm a thyroid problem. The NHS describes an underactive thyroid as common and usually lifelong, and says it can be managed with medicine. Hashimoto's disease, the main cause, is often stable for years, according to MedlinePlus.

sections.heading: What causes an underactive thyroid?
sections.body:
The main cause in the UK is Hashimoto's disease, which is an autoimmune condition. Autoimmune means the body's defence system mistakenly attacks its own tissue, in this case the thyroid. The NIDDK says most people with Hashimoto's disease go on to develop an underactive thyroid. Inflammation of the thyroid, called thyroiditis, is another cause.

Surgery or radiotherapy around the neck or thyroid can also lead to it. Treatment for an overactive thyroid can lead to it as well. The NIDDK explains that radioactive iodine gradually destroys thyroid cells, so people given it will probably eventually develop an underactive thyroid. Certain medicines, including lithium, amiodarone and interferons, have been linked to the condition. Some babies are born with an underactive thyroid, which is called congenital hypothyroidism.

sections.heading: What happens at an appointment, and which tests are used?
sections.body:
A GP will ask about symptoms and family history, and may examine the neck. The blood test is a standard one that does not need fasting, and it measures thyroid hormone levels. TSH is a hormone made by the pituitary gland that tells the thyroid how much to produce. A high level of TSH together with a low level of thyroid hormone (T4) can point to an underactive thyroid.

When Hashimoto's disease is suspected, the NIDDK says doctors usually also check for thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies. These antibodies are present in most people with Hashimoto's disease. An ultrasound scan may be used if antibodies are not found but Hashimoto's disease is still suspected. MedlinePlus says scans and biopsies are generally not needed to make the diagnosis. The results are explained by the clinician, who decides whether treatment is needed.

sections.heading: How is an underactive thyroid treated?
sections.body:
The usual treatment is levothyroxine tablets. Levothyroxine is identical to the thyroid hormone thyroxine, also known as T4, that the body makes naturally. The NHS says people usually need to take it for the rest of their lives to stop symptoms coming back. Some people with very mild symptoms, or none, may not need any treatment.

Regular blood tests are used at the start until the right dose is found, and this can take a while to get right. After a dose is started or changed, a follow-up blood test is usually arranged some weeks later. The NIDDK says the condition can be well controlled as long as the medicine is taken as the doctor directs and the follow-up blood tests are attended. It also warns that too much thyroid hormone medicine can cause serious problems, such as an irregular heart rhythm called atrial fibrillation, or weak bones.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, babies and children
sections.body:
The NHS advises telling the GP when pregnant or trying to conceive with an underactive thyroid. Further tests are needed, and the levothyroxine dose will probably change during pregnancy. Thyroid blood test results naturally change a little as a pregnancy goes on. Untreated, an underactive thyroid in pregnancy can raise the chance of problems such as pre-eclampsia, birth defects, premature birth or miscarriage. After the birth, the dose needed usually returns to normal, so most women go back to their earlier dose.

Some babies are born with an underactive thyroid, called congenital hypothyroidism. Its signs can be subtle at birth, which is why newborn screening matters. A clinical review reports that treatment started after screening supports normal growth and development. Some babies have a temporary form of the condition. Another review says some children treated early still have mild hearing difficulties, so periodic checks of development, school progress and hearing are recommended.

sections.heading: What are the complications and the outlook?
sections.body:
The NHS says an underactive thyroid is not usually serious when it is treated properly. Untreated or poorly controlled, it can raise the risk of heart problems and of bone problems such as osteoporosis. The NHS also lists goitre, which is an enlarged thyroid gland, and problems in pregnancy as possible complications.

Myxoedema coma is a very rare but life-threatening complication that needs emergency hospital treatment. In an emergency, such as someone with a known underactive thyroid who becomes very drowsy or confused, the route is to call 999. Ongoing symptoms during treatment are a reason to book a routine GP appointment, since blood tests are used to check that the dose is right.
